flashcards.q: What can an input guardrail catch that an output guardrail cannot, and vice versa?
flashcards.a: Input rails see the request before generation and block known-bad patterns before the model runs, but can't see what would have been generated. Output rails see the actual response but only after generation, so a tool-call side effect has already happened by the time they check.

flashcards.q: Name the six guardrail layers and one thing each catches.
flashcards.a: Schema validation (malformed structured output), PII detection/redaction (named-entity PII), toxicity classifiers (overtly harmful language), topical restriction (off-domain requests), jailbreak detection (known attack patterns), groundedness checks (claims not traceable to RAG sources).

flashcards.q: What's the industry latency budget target for input and output rails, and where does the stack become the bottleneck?
flashcards.a: Sub-100ms p50 for input, sub-150ms p50 for output. 200ms p50 is the threshold where the guardrail stack becomes the product's latency bottleneck.

flashcards.q: Give the latency range for an LLM-based guardrail validator, and its cost impact.
flashcards.a: 200-800ms added latency, plus roughly 15-40% added to the provider bill per turn.

flashcards.q: What's Llama Guard 4's measured p95 latency on typical GPU hardware?
What are the industry-typical catch rate and false-positive rate ranges for guardrail frameworks?
flashcards.a: 60-85% catch rate on problems a human would classify as serious, and 5-15% false positives on legitimate turns.

flashcards.q: Why is false-positive rate the metric that decides whether a guardrail survives in production, not catch rate?
flashcards.a: Catch rate is what you tune in a demo; a high false-positive rate generates daily user friction and support load, which leads teams to loosen thresholds under pressure and often forget to re-tighten, silently eroding protection.

flashcards.q: When should a guardrail fail-closed vs fail-open on its own error?
flashcards.a: Fail-closed for regulated/high-stakes domains (healthcare, finance, legal exposure) where an unfiltered response is unacceptable even at the cost of availability. Fail-open for low-stakes paths, especially where a stronger downstream control already covers the real risk.

flashcards.q: Why do most open-source guardrail libraries default to fail-open, and why is that dangerous?
flashcards.a: Fail-open avoids paging anyone when the classifier goes down. It's dangerous because teams inherit this default without realizing they made a compliance decision by not making one explicitly for their domain.

flashcards.q: Describe the canonical 'guardrails as theatre' failure.
flashcards.a: An agent leaks data via a tool call (email, API write, log line), then produces an innocuous text summary like 'data exported successfully.' An output filter scanning only the chat response reports clean because it never saw the tool call where the leak actually happened.

flashcards.q: Contrast NeMo Guardrails, Guardrails AI, and Llama Guard architecturally.
flashcards.a: NeMo Guardrails: programmable Colang rails (input/output/dialog/retrieval/execution) running in-process, under 50ms on GPU. Guardrails AI: Pydantic-based Guard + validator Hub (50+ validators), 50-200ms per validator. Llama Guard: a standalone classifier model returning safe/unsafe plus a category, not a framework.

flashcards.q: What does a groundedness check verify, and what can't it catch?
flashcards.a: It verifies that response claims trace back to the retrieved source documents — the core defense against RAG hallucination. It can't catch hallucination with nothing to ground against, and can't catch a claim that's technically traceable to a source that is itself wrong.

flashcards.q: Name three cloud-managed guardrail products and one distinguishing feature each.
flashcards.a: AWS Bedrock Guardrails (model-agnostic policy layer via ApplyGuardrail API); Azure AI Content Safety (Prompt Shields for jailbreak/indirect-injection detection, plus groundedness detection); Google Model Armor (prompt/response inspection and safety filtering).

flashcards.q: Why does a jailbreak detector's effectiveness decay over time even without any code changes?
flashcards.a: Jailbreak/injection classifiers are adversarial targets; attackers iterate against known detectors the way they iterate against WAF rules, so a static classifier's real-world catch rate drops as new phrasings are discovered and shared.

flashcards.q: Give a case where adding an available, cheap guardrail layer is still the wrong call.
flashcards.a: When it duplicates coverage a stronger control already provides (e.g. a text PII filter behind a system with no tool that could leak PII), since every added layer compounds false-positive odds across the stack for no matching threat.
